notes: Rate is usually quoted per $100 of coverage.

explanation: [[kw:Fire insurance]] provides protection against loss by fire, lightning, and often extended coverage perils (windstorm, hail, explosion).
The [[kw:face amount]] of the policy is the maximum the insurer will pay for a covered loss.
[[kw:Premium]] is calculated per $100 of insurance: $$\frac{\text{Face Amount}}{100} \times \text{Rate per } \$100$$
Rates depend on factors like building construction (frame, brick), occupancy type, and fire protection available.

steps: Without coinsurance, owners might underinsure to save on premiums, knowing partial losses are more common.

It makes insurance fairer for all policyholders.

confusionCorner.body: The coinsurance formula applies only to partial losses. [[imp:If the loss equals or exceeds the face amount, the insurer pays the face amount, not the coinsurance amount.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

explanation: A [[kw:coinsurance clause]] requires the insured to carry insurance equal to at least a specified percentage (usually 80%) of the property's value at the time of loss.
If the insurance carried is less than the required amount, the recovery for a partial loss is reduced by the formula:
$$\text{Amount Paid} = \frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Insurance Required}} \times \text{Loss}$$
where Insurance Required = Property Value × Coinsurance Percentage.
[[imp:Coinsurance encourages property owners to insure to full value or at least the required percentage.]]

notes: The payment cannot exceed the face amount of the policy.
If the loss equals or exceeds the face amount, the formula may be capped.

blocks.title: 3. Cancellation and Premium Refunds

discoveryHook.scenario: A business cancels its $1,200 annual fire policy after 5 months. The insurer uses a short‑rate table: for 5 months, the earned premium is 50%. The unearned 50% is refunded: $1,200 × 0.50 = $600. If the insurer cancels, a pro‑rata refund applies: 7/12 of $1,200 = $700.

visuals.caption: Short‑rate gives less refund because of penalty.
visuals.title: Cancellation Refund Comparison ($1,200 annual premium, cancel after 5 months)

notes: Short‑rate factor is from a table; it represents earned premium as a percent.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Short‑Rate Refund} = \text{Annual Premium} \times (1 - \text{Short‑Rate Factor})$$ $$\text{Pro‑Rata Refund} = \text{Annual Premium} \times \frac{\text{Remaining Months}}{12}$$
formulaCard.title: Cancellation Refund

explanation: If the insured cancels, the refund is based on a [[kw:short‑rate table]], which charges a penalty for early cancellation.
If the insurer cancels, the refund is [[kw:pro‑rata]], meaning the unearned premium is returned proportionally to the remaining time.
Short‑rate refund = Annual premium × (1 – Short‑rate factor for the time policy was in force).
Pro‑rata refund = Annual premium × (Remaining months / 12).
[[imp:The short‑rate refund is always less than the pro‑rata refund for the same period.]]

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Short‑rate tables vary by company; always refer to the specific table provided. [[imp:If no table is given, use the pro‑rata method.]]

visuals.caption: ACV leaves a gap that replacement cost coverage can fill.

explanation: [[kw:Actual cash value (ACV)]] = Replacement cost – Depreciation.
Standard fire policies pay ACV, not replacement cost, unless a replacement cost endorsement is added.
In a total loss within policy limits, the insurer pays the face amount or ACV, whichever is less.
[[kw:Replacement cost coverage]] pays the amount to replace the property with new materials of like kind and quality, without deduction for depreciation.

formulaCard.title: Fire Insurance Blueprint

explanation: Apply the blueprint to fire insurance problems:
1. Understand: identify face amount, property value, coinsurance percentage, loss amount, premium rate if needed.
2. Solve: compute required insurance; if coinsurance, compare carried to required and apply formula. If premium, compute premium. If cancellation, compute refund.
3. Conclude: state the payment or refund; advise whether the insured is compliant or underinsured.
This structured approach separates coverage analysis from arithmetic.
